abstract: Technology-mediated service interactions, such as phone calls, generate rich behavioral signals that firms currently struggle to monitor in real time. Post-interaction surveys provide delayed and unrepresentative feedback, leaving satisfaction invisible as calls unfold. Satisfaction judgments depend on how evaluative meaning is communicated across two channels, verbal content and vocal delivery, whose relative contribution varies by outcome type. The authors analyze 1,144 real-world service calls, each coded as dissatisfied, neutral, or satisfied, using text-only, audio-only, and multimodal deep learning models. Dissatisfied calls are identified from transcripts alone as accurately as by multimodal models, since customers articulate problems and remedy expectations explicitly. Neutral and satisfied calls depend more strongly on vocal interpretation, and cross-attention models outperform text-only alternatives precisely where verbal content is absent or insufficiently distinctive to separate outcomes. The findings identify a boundary condition on interactivity, whereby vocal cues add predictive value when evaluative meaning is absent or insufficiently distinctive between outcomes, not when it is explicit and clearly distinguishes outcomes, as is the case for dissatisfied calls.

ur.ai_reason: 以深度学习分析真实服务电话与满意度
ur.tldr: 分析1,144通真实客服电话，以文本、音频及跨注意力多模态模型识别满意状态。不满可由明确表述准确识别；中立与满意更依赖语调，语音线索仅在语言信息不足或区分度低时增加预测价值。

title: EXPRESS: THE SOUND OF WORDS: VERBAL AND VOCAL CUES IN CUSTOMER SATISFACTION
title_zh: EXPRESS：词语之声：客户满意度中的语言与声音线索
